Rites of Passage Poland Pavilion at Gwangju Biennale 2026 September 5–November 15, 2026 Add to Calendar Opening: September 5, 4:30pm, followed by a live concert and performance of White Smile by Anna Zaradny at 5:30pm Gwangju Biennale 111 Biennale-ro, Buk-gu Gwangju 61104 South Korea iam.pl Facebook / Instagram What happens when one chapter of life has come to an end, but the next has yet to begin? This is the question at the heart of Rites of Passage , an exhibition organised by the Adam Mickiewicz Institute for the Poland Pavilion at 16th Gwangju Biennale , one of the most important contemporary art events in Asia. The exhibition opens on September 5, 2026 at Leeleenam Studio in Gwangju (10, Jejung-ro 47beon-gil, Nam-gu, Gwangju 61642, Yangnim District, Republic of Korea) with the official opening at 4:30pm, followed by a live concert and performance of White Smile by Anna Zaradny at 5:30pm. The project curated by Paulina Olszewska explores the experience of transition—both on a personal and a global scale. It brings together artists from Poland and Korea: Alicja Bielawska , Urszula Broll , Inside Job (Ula Lucińska and Michał Knychaus ) , Park Saengkwang , Yeesookyung , and Anna Zaradny . We live in a time of constant flux, yet we increasingly lack shared rituals that help us navigate through it. What was once embedded in the rhythm of communal life—transitions between life stages, mourning, coming of age, the beginning of a new chapter—has often become a private experience, difficult to articulate. It is precisely this condition that Rites of Passage seeks to explore. The exhibition takes as its starting point a passage from The White Book , written by Han Kang during her stay in Warsaw in 2016. In it, the author reflects on a moment of hesitation: the threshold between what has already happened and what is yet to come. It is a moment of uncertainty, anticipation, and stepping into the unknown. For curator Paulina Olszewska, this image became the starting point for a broader reflection on rites of passage—those moments when our lives change, sometimes dramatically, sometimes almost imperceptibly . From birth to death, from personal decisions to historical turning points, change is a constant presence. It shapes our everyday lives, memory, relationships, and communities. The rite of passage is not merely the subject of the exhibition—it is also embedded in its spatial design. Visitors will move through a sequence of environments, ranging from spaces of subtle, almost imperceptible transformation to areas defined by distinct thresholds, tensions, and ruptures. In one section, the artworks will gently merge into one another, suggesting change as a gradual process. In another, visitors will encounter contrast, dissonance, and a sense of disruption. The journey through the pavilion becomes a physical experience of crossing a threshold—of moving from one state of being to another. The exhibition also responds to the theme of the 16th Gwangju Biennale, You Must Change Your Life . In a world marked by war, the climate crisis, social tensions, and increasing polarisation, transformation is no abstract concept. It is something we experience every day—in our private lives, in politics, in society, and in our relationships with others. The exhibition brings together different generations, artistic traditions, and media. Traditional painting and drawing meet installation, video, sound, ceramics, textiles, and objects made from both organic and industrial materials. Works by Alicja Bielawska , Inside Job , and Anna Zaradny are presented in dialogue with historical works by Urszula Broll and Park Saengkwang —widely regarded as one of the leading figures of modern Korean art, whose work has become an enduring part of Korea’s cultural heritage—as well as an installation by Yeesookyung . Together, they create a multisensory environment in which materials, images, sounds, and textures evoke an atmosphere of contemplation, suspension, and transformation. A specially commissioned sound composition will form an integral part of the exhibition. Rooted in the traditional music of the region while incorporating experimental approaches to sound, it will serve as an acoustic guide through the exhibition—a sonic landscape accompanying visitors as they move through the successive spaces of the pavilion. Rites of Passage has been conceived as an open exhibition, without providing a single prescribed narrative or any straightforward answers. Each visitor is invited to experience it in their own way, interpreting its symbols, tensions, and transitions through the lens of their own sensibility. It is a space for contemplation: intimate and personal, yet deeply attentive to the contemporary world. Viewed through both Polish and Korean perspectives, the exhibition becomes a shared meditation on change—inevitable, unsettling, yet profoundly human. It will be on view as part of the Biennale until 15 November 2026 . Press materials and high-resolution images are available at the following link . The Poland Pavilion at Gwangju Biennale is organised by the Adam Mickiewicz Institute with support from the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in Seoul, the ING Polish Art Foundation, Leeleenam Studio and Galeria Studio . Project is funded by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage of the Republic of Poland. The Adam Mickiewicz Institute (IAM) brings Polish culture to people around the world. Being a state institution, it creates lasting interest in Polish culture and art through strengthening the presence of Polish artists on the global stage. It initiates innovative projects, supports international cooperation and cultural exchanges. It promotes the work of both established and promising artists, showing the diversity and richness of our culture. The Adam Mickiewicz Institute is also responsible for the Culture.pl website, which is a comprehensive source of knowledge about Polish culture. More information here . https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oc.text: Rules in Covent Garden. Owner JP Mayhew donated the restaurant to the National Trust, saying it will ‘protect this place in a way that no one else could’. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Rules in Covent Garden. Owner JP Mayhew donated the restaurant to the National Trust, saying it will ‘protect this place in a way that no one else could’. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian Restaurants Rules, London’s oldest restaurant, donated to National Trust Historic eatery in capital’s theatreland given to heritage charity after changing hands only three times in 228 years Esther Addley and George Francis Lee Tue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google When Thomas Rule served his first oyster to diners on Maiden Lane in London’s Covent Garden, “mad” George III was on the throne of England, John Adams was US president and William Pitt the Younger had just come up with a wheeze called income tax to pay for the Napoleonic wars. More than two centuries later, Rules , the restaurant Thomas founded in what became the capital’s theatreland, has outlasted nine British monarchs and 45 prime ministers – but has changed hands only three times. The interior of its four-storey home, stuffed with historic playbills and vintage caricatures and gilded antlers, is little changed from the 19th century, nor has the tone of its determinedly meaty menu – think rabbit rillettes, shin of veal and roast guinea fowl. View image in fullscreen Established in 1798, Rules was once frequented by the likes of Charles Dickens, Laurence Olivier and Charlie Chaplin. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian Rules was beloved by Dickens and Thackeray, inspired Graham Greene and was a favourite of Charlie Chaplin, Laurence Olivier and Ava Gardner. But even London’s oldest restaurant can feel vulnerable to the winds of change, leading the man who bought Rules in 1984 to take perhaps the most significant step in its long history. JP Mayhew has now donated the restaurant’s historic home to the National Trust , assured that the heritage charity will “protect this place in a way that no one else could”. “With many years of hard work, and some extraordinary strokes of luck, Rules has survived everything from redevelopment plans and changing tastes to the blitz ,” Mayhew said. By taking on the historic and listed 34- 35 Maiden Lane , he added , the National Trust would “[safeguard] its bricks and mortar, its famous interior and its invisible atmosphere too. I am grateful to them for believing in this idea and for protecting this building and two centuries worth of stories for people to enjoy forever”. View image in fullscreen The interior of its four-storey home, stuffed with historic playbills and vintage caricatures and gilded antlers, is little changed from the 19th century. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian The £11m “landmark” gift is one of the most valuable in the National Trust’s recent history, and will mark its first entry into the restaurant business – although its portfolio includes 39 historic pubs and a number of country house hotels, including Cliveden in Buckinghamshire. Not that the heritage charity will be taking on the napkin-folding and the slow cooking of pork cheeks. While Mayhew is donating the historic building and its contents, he sold the restaurant business to Ricky McMenemy , its longstanding general manager, in 2022; McMenemy will become a commercial tenant of the National Trust. View image in fullscreen Diners can expect little change to the menu, said Lucy Porten from the National Trust: ‘It’s not a National Trust menu … there will be no scones.’ Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian “Our involvement, day to day, will probably be very light touch,” said Lucy Porten, a national curator for the charity. “It will always be run as a restaurant. We will look after [the building and its contents], but we recognise that they will have to evolve if they are going to continue to meet diners’ needs.” Diners, however, can expect little change to the menu, she said – and crucially, no scones. “It’s not a National Trust menu, this is a very successful business in its own right. There will be no scones. That’s not their business.” Nor will there be preferential access or prices for National Trust members, “because it is a business, and it has to be successful,” she added. Instead, the charity is exploring options for virtual visits and other ways people could “feel like they are visiting the space” from afar. It was several years ago when Mayhew first approached the National Trust about a possible gift. Porten said while “excited by the offer”, they looked carefully at whether it was the right organisation to take on the building. View image in fullscreen The storied restaurant has outlasted nine British monarchs and 45 prime ministers. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian Porten said: “The nature of the National Trust, and the fact we have this extraordinary ability to take on places inalienably, for ever, means that we have to think about what’s right for now, but also to think about looking after them for future generations. That’s quite a big thing … It had to be quite a balanced response and decision.” Part of its value to the trust, she said, lay in helping the charity “tell different histories which are hard for us to tell at our other properties”. “You get a sense of all the delicious food which has been enjoyed here, the fine wines that have been consumed, the good company that’s been enjoyed. There’s something in the air about the conversations and the celebrations, the flirtations, the deals that have been struck, the heartbreak. All that hangs in the air, in a very magical way, [as] the backdrop to lots of different historical moments and lives. “It’s an extraordinary slice of the social history of London, and to have been here for so long - in this site and doing this business – is a very rare and special thing.” Explore more on these topics Restaurants The National Trust Food Heritage London news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/iran.text: Iranul a prezentat marți, 10 noiembrie, o nouă bază militară subterană, denumită „oraș al rachetelor”, în care sunt depozitate rachete balistice, rachete de croazieră și sisteme de lansare. Dezvăluirea instalației militare are loc pe fondul tensiunilor cu Statele Unite și Israelul, iar conducerea armatei iraniene avertizează că dispune de capacități militare care ar putea surprinde adversarii într-un eventual nou conflict. Noua instalație aparține Forței Aerospațiale a Corpului Gardienilor Revoluției Islamice (IRGC), una dintre cele mai importante structuri militare ale Iranului, scrie Yahoo News. Potrivit imaginilor difuzate de agențiile de presă iraniene, complexul cuprinde tuneluri subterane în care sunt amplasate diferite tipuri de rachete și lansatoare. Autoritățile nu au precizat locația exactă a instalației și nici capacitatea acesteia. La prezentare au participat generalul-maior Ali Abdollahi, șeful Statului Major al forțelor armate iraniene, și generalul de brigadă Seyed Majid Mousavi, comandantul Forței Aerospațiale a Gardienilor Revoluției. Oficialii au inspectat instalațiile și au evaluat capacitatea operațională a unităților responsabile de utilizarea rachetelor. Setarile tale privind cookie-urile nu permit afisarea continutul din aceasta sectiune. Poti actualiza setarile modulelor coookie direct din browser sau de aici – e nevoie sa accepti cookie-urile social media Prezentarea bazei subterane a fost anunțată încă din 7 noiembrie de purtătorul de cuvânt al Gardienilor Revoluției, generalul Hossein Mohebbi. Acesta a susținut că Iranul și-a transferat rapid o parte dintre liniile de producție a rachetelor și dronelor din instalațiile de la suprafață în complexe subterane, pentru a le proteja împotriva atacurilor aeriene. Potrivit oficialului iranian, Teheranul nu se mai limitează la construirea unor depozite subterane pentru armament, ci dezvoltă și facilități de producție amplasate la mare adâncime. Mohebbi a afirmat că infrastructura industrială și capacitățile tehnice ale Iranului ar permite continuarea fabricării armamentului chiar și în condițiile unor bombardamente intense. Afirmațiile autorităților iraniene privind amploarea infrastructurii și capacitatea acesteia de a rezista atacurilor nu au putut fi verificate independent. În timpul vizitei, generalul Ali Abdollahi a transmis un avertisment Statelor Unite și Israelului, afirmând că noile capacități militare ale Iranului ar putea avea un impact neașteptat pe câmpul de luptă. „Surprizele din următorul război vor fi dezvăluite una după alta”, a declarat comandantul iranian, potrivit televiziunii de stat Press TV. Abdollahi a susținut că forțele iraniene au demonstrat deja că pot rezista unor operațiuni militare desfășurate cu armament american avansat. Potrivit acestuia, capacitatea de rezistență a Iranului nu depinde exclusiv de tehnologia militară, ci și de determinarea personalului implicat în apărarea țării. Dezvăluirea noului complex subteran are loc într-un moment în care Iranul încearcă să demonstreze că își poate menține capacitățile militare după confruntările cu Statele Unite și Israelul. Construirea unor asemenea instalații reprezintă o componentă importantă a strategiei militare iraniene. Amplasarea rachetelor, lansatoarelor și unităților de producție în subteran urmărește reducerea vulnerabilității acestora în fața atacurilor aeriene. În paralel, Teheranul continuă să investească în infrastructura necesară producerii și utilizării rachetelor balistice și de croazieră. Anunțul vine și în contextul unor declarații ale președintelui american Donald Trump privind perspectivele unui acord cu Iranul, în timp ce autoritățile de la Teheran insistă că programul lor de rachete rămâne operațional. Prin prezentarea noului „oraș al rachetelor”, conducerea iraniană încearcă să transmită că dispune în continuare de mijloacele necesare pentru a răspunde unei eventuale noi operațiuni militare americane sau israeliene.
